title: How to Distinguish Drone Swarms, Flocks of Birds and Alien Technology in UAP Data?

--

When studying Unidentified Anomalous Phenomena (UAP) in the eight tranches of data released by the Presidential Unsealing and Reporting System for UAP Encounters (PURSUE) here, it is important to separate the wheat from the chaff. The chaff contains terrestrial objects in the form of drones and birds which move in clusters. Separating technological from biological signatures is key to identifying UAP of potentially extraterrestrial origin.

In a new paper that I co-authored with Volkan Duran and Omer Eldadi here, we attempted to find out whether video of objects in the sky can show how a group of them is controlled, a question raised by the Search for Extraterrestrial Artificial Intelligence (SETAI), outlined in my previous work here. Our method sets four conditions that a recording must meet before birds can be separated from drones and learning machines: (i) the delay of each response must be measurable; (ii) members must be located in three dimensions so that neighbors can be identified; (iii) the recording must include situations in which these controllers behave differently; and (iv) the fixed-rule model used for comparison must be declared in advance. Our paper tests each condition on data in which the controller is known. The data come from the Galileo Observatory in Las Vegas, where we compare infrared video of birds with a choreographed show of several hundred drones over the Las Vegas Sphere, and from public datasets on simulated mosquito swarms, jackdaw and chimney-swift flocks, bat pairs and honeybees. We conclude that alignment does not separate birds from drones, since both flew in highly aligned groups. Instead, wingbeat flicker identified the birds (as discussed by Jacob Haqq-Misra et al. 2026). Flock interactions require triangulation from several cameras. Repeated identical fluctuations can make a fixed script look like learning. In existing data from the Galileo Project, the cameras are too far apart to triangulate birds which can only be noticed at close proximity to only one of the cameras.

SETAI asks two questions about an anomalous object: is it technological, and if so, what controls it? The first is ranked on the 0–10 Loeb Scale, as defined in a previous paper here. Our previous paper, described here, proposed two tools for the second question. An evidence gate (E1–E6) checks that an object has been located, that ordinary explanations such as birds or aircraft have been tested and that the data can be traced to their source. A four-level SETAI Control Scale (C0–C3) then grades the evidence about control, from C0, where control cannot be assessed, to C3, where the evidence favors a controller that updates its behavior from experience. Each grade is judged against three reference hypotheses: biological direction (B), as in a flock of birds; scripted automation (S), as in a drone light show that follows a pre-written flight plan; and adaptive autonomy (A), as in a machine that changes its rules with experience. Timing and operating-envelope tests (T1–T2) can exclude biological limits, and a disruption–response test (T3) compares a controller that updates after a disturbance with a fixed-rule model of declared complexity. Each grade also carries an origin flag (T, terrestrial; U, undetermined; X, extrasolar). Groups of UAP can be filmed in motion, but their origin is often undetermined. Our goal is to identify what a video recording must contain before it can show how a group of flying objects is controlled, and to apply that test to birds and drones filmed by the Galileo Observatory in Las Vegas. The question arises because very different controllers can produce similar motion. Birds in a flock turn together because each bird reacts to its neighbors. The drones of a light show turn together because each follows its own part of a pre-written flight plan. An autonomous drone swarm may follow fixed local rules or change them with experience. We tested four conditions on data with known controllers and applied them to Galileo recordings of birds and of a choreographed drone show. The recordings identify the objects but do not yet reveal how they are controlled, and the reference data show which condition fails and why. The drone show illustrates why silhouette matters. Hovering drones modulated less than most birds, but codec lines at 12 Hz and aliased rotor modulations overlapped the weakest bird line when sources were unresolved, so a wingbeat resolved in the silhouette is a more specific sign of a bird than the brightness of an unresolved source.

The mosquito benchmark shows that a rule can be present and still be invisible in global summaries: swarm averages missed the known collision-avoidance rule, whereas close-encounter acceleration and closest approach detected it. What is still missing experimentally is a labelled, unscheduled disturbance that brings the group into the states that separate the declared models. The supplementary pigeon contrast provides ecological context but does not address this requirement. Distance matters for control because neighbor relations depend on it. A single camera limits the neighbor structure that can be recovered.

For the Galileo Observatory, the next observational step is a three-dimensional record of a bird flock from synchronized, calibrated cameras, with the same birds identified in each view and a 3D uncertainty for each track. The present layout is not suited to this as its sites are 2.0 and 10.1 km apart, so a flock seen from two of them is a few kilometers away, where neighboring birds merge within a pixel and birds are fainter than the sensitivity of the cameras. A closely spaced triangle of cameras a few hundred meters apart, designed for this purpose, would avoid both problems. A second step is a pre-registered field experiment in the field of view of the Las Vegas array, with drones flown under declared replay, fixed-feedback and learning-enabled controllers. Operators would retain controller code and logs, label safe unscheduled disruptions and withhold perturbation types from fitting, and assessors would be blinded to controller identity. Such an experiment would calibrate the instrument on locally acquired known-answer data. Separately, the Sphere operator’s flight plan and execution logs would test the assumed choreography and could provide an exact script-based negative control.

This study asked whether video of objects in the sky can show how a group of them is controlled. We stated four conditions that a recording must meet: the response delay must be measurable; neighbors and the order of turning must survive the camera views and the errors of triangulation; the record must contain the situations that separate the candidate controllers, reached through a labelled external disturbance rather than by chance; and the fixed-rule comparison model must be declared in advance and protected against under-declared scripts and the adaptation mirage. Public data with known controllers tested timing, neighbor structure, visitation of rule-relevant states and the comparison model; the full T3 test of external disturbance and updating remains prospective. In the Galileo Observatory recordings, the objects in the five clips are birds (E3), and the Sphere show is choreographed drones with an unverified flight script. Both stay at C0, because each was filmed by a single camera and met no unplanned disturbance. Telling birds from drones by how they are controlled will require triangulated positions, which the present sites, kilometers apart, cannot provide for bird flocks. The practical route is a closely spaced camera triangle or narrow-field (about 5°) tracking cameras beside the wide-field all-sky arrays, calibrated on drones flown under declared controllers in their field of view.

ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Avi Loeb is chair of the UAP Science Advisory Council to the White House, Pentagon, FBI and intelligence agencies, director of the Galileo Project, founding director of Harvard University’s — Black Hole Initiative (2016–2021), former director of the Institute for Theory and Computation at the Harvard-Smithsonian Center for Astrophysics (2005–2026), and the former chair of the astronomy department at Harvard University (2011–2020). He is a former member of the President’s Council of Advisors on Science and Technology (2018–2019) and a former chair of the Board on Physics and Astronomy of the National Academies (2018–2021). He is the bestselling author of “Extraterrestrial: The First Sign of Intelligent Life Beyond Earth” and a co-author of the textbook “Life in the Cosmos”, both published in 2021. The paperback edition of his new book, titled “Interstellar”, was published in August 2024.
